Your instinct is half-right, and for pnpm specifically the `--` is worse than unnecessary — it actively breaks things.

Results on your machine (pnpm 9.15.9, npm 11.6.2):

| Command | Script receives |
|---|---|
| `pnpm run show /bookshelf/` | `/bookshelf/` |
| `pnpm run show -- /bookshelf/` | `--` `/bookshelf/` ← **`--` leaks through** |
| `pnpm run show --preset=desktop` | `--preset=desktop` |
| `npm run show /bookshelf/` | `/bookshelf/` |
| `npm run show --preset=desktop` | *(nothing — npm ate it)* |
| `npm run show -- --preset=desktop` | `--preset=desktop` |

So the real rule isn't "scripts can't take args." It's:

- **Positional args always forwarded**, in both npm and pnpm. `npm run perf /bookshelf/` would have worked all along.
- **The `--` exists for flag-shaped args**, and only in npm. `npm run perf --preset=desktop` — npm parses `--preset` as its own option and swallows it. `--` says "stop parsing, rest is the script's."
- **pnpm doesn't need it and doesn't strip it.** pnpm forwards everything after the script name verbatim, so a habitual `--` arrives as a literal `$1`.

That last row is the trap. `pnpm perf -- /bookshelf/` would set `PATH_ARG="--"` and Lighthouse would go hit `http://localhost:9999/--`. Since that's an easy reflex, I added a guard:

great. Can you explain `decoding="async"`?

It's a hint about **decoding** — turning the compressed WebP bytes into a bitmap — not about downloading.

Three separate knobs, easy to conflate:

| Attribute | Controls |
|---|---|
| `loading` | *when* the fetch starts |
| `fetchpriority` | network priority of the fetch |
| `decoding` | when the decode happens relative to painting |

Values are `sync`, `async`, `auto` (default). `async` tells the browser it may present surrounding content without waiting for this image to finish decoding. `sync` asks for the opposite — decode it atomically with the rest, so it appears in the same frame as its neighbors.

The reasoning for 56 images: decoding is CPU work, and a burst of it can block the main thread and jank the page. `async` says none of these are worth stalling a paint for.

Honest caveat: browsers already decode off the main thread in most cases, so this is closer to a nudge than a guarantee, and on a lot of pages it measures as a no-op. It's most defensible where it is here — many images, all decorative, none of them the LCP element. If you'd rather not carry an attribute you can't observe doing anything, dropping it is reasonable.

Short answer: no. Right now every one of them fetches on load. There's no `loading` attribute on the `img`, so they're `eager` — the browser fetches unconditionally the moment it parses the tag. Visibility plays no part in that decision. None of these stop an eager fetch: - clipped by an ancestor's `overflow: hidden` - `visibility: hidden` or `opacity: 0` - fully covered by another element - even `display: none` — that suppresses a CSS `background-image`, but not an `` The only built-in mechanism that skips them is `loading="lazy"`, and it keys off **viewport proximity**, not actual visibility. So it doesn't quite answer your case: an image that's above the fold but hidden is still near the viewport, and lazy will happily load it. Where lazy does help is content clipped out of a scroll container — that genuinely doesn't intersect, so it's deferred until you scroll. Note the thresholds are generous; Chrome starts fetching well before something enters view, so it's a coarse tool. The practical shape of this: with `auto-fit` you don't know at build time how many pieces land in the first row, so you can't mark "row one eager, rest lazy." If you later move to a fixed column count for the conveyor, you would know, and that split becomes easy. Worth noting the scale — 56 pieces is about 500KB and 56 connections to `stuff.tylergaw.com`. Both are global CDNs over HTTP/2, so raw delivery speed is close to a wash. The differences are elsewhere:

| | In-repo (Netlify) | Bucket (S3 + CloudFront) |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | Reuses the page's existing one | Separate origin (now preconnected) |
| `Cache-Control` | `public,max-age=0,must-revalidate` | **none sent** |
| Repeat visit | Conditional request → 304, no bytes | Heuristic caching, unpredictable |

**Same-origin's structural edge** is that images ride the connection the HTML already opened — no DNS, TCP, or TLS at all. The preconnect narrows that gap; it doesn't close it. On a page pulling one or two images, this is noise. On a page pulling 56, the handshake is amortized across all of them and stops mattering much either way.

**The actual lever is `Cache-Control`, and neither host is doing well.** Netlify's `max-age=0,must-revalidate` means every image is revalidated on every visit — cheap 304s, no bytes, but still a round trip each. The bucket sends no cache header at all, so browsers fall back to heuristics based on `Last-Modified`; since that file was modified minutes ago, the heuristic window is effectively nothing. Fixing headers on either host beats moving files between them.

Netlify's default isn't timidity — your image paths aren't content-hashed, so a long `max-age` means overwriting `foo.webp` leaves users on the old one indefinitely. Long caching requires either hashed filenames or a rule that you never reuse a path. Same constraint applies to the bucket.

**So I'd decide this on repo hygiene, not perf.** Binary files in git are permanent — they never leave the history, and every clone pays for them forever. That's the real argument for pushing the 56 pieces, videos, and future heavy media to the bucket. Keep small structural site chrome in the repo, where it's versioned alongside the code that uses it and costs no handshake.

content.text:
## The shared system

Four classes, all defined in [tylergaw.css:499-545](src/css/tylergaw.css:499) inside `@layer components`.

| Class | What it does |
|---|---|
| `hero--before-standard` | Creates a positioned `::before` — the main colored slab behind the hero |
| `hero--after-standard` | Same for `::after` — a second decorative slab |
| `hero--offset` | Pulls the whole hero up under the header via `translateY` + negative `margin-bottom` |
| `hero__contents` | `position: relative; z-index: 1` — keeps real content above the slabs |

## How it works

The two pseudo-element classes share a base rule that sets `content: ""`, `display: block`, `position: absolute`, then defines two custom properties the project stylesheets consume:

- `--gutter: 1rem` — horizontal inset. `left: var(--gutter)`, `width: calc(100% - var(--gutter) * 2)`. Only defined here, nowhere else in the codebase.
- `--offset-v: calc(var(--gutter) * 3)` — vertical breathing room. `hero--before-standard::before` defaults to `height: calc(100% - var(--offset-v))`.

At 620px the gutter doubles (`calc(var(--gutter) * 2)`). `hero--offset` ramps its pull across three steps: `-0.5rem` → `-1.25rem` at 620 → `-2.3rem` at 730.

The division of labor: **the shared classes handle geometry only** — position, inset, height, stacking. Each project stylesheet supplies the paint. Every project's `.hero--<name>` sets `position: relative` (the anchor the absolute pseudo-elements need) plus a text color, then overrides the pseudo-elements with `background`, `clip-path`, `mask`, `transform`.

## Where they're used

Five work pages, all with the same class stack except JXA:

| Page | Classes |
|---|---|
| [colorme.webc:22](src/work/colorme.webc:22) | before + after + offset |
| [limbo.webc:16](src/work/limbo.webc:16) | before + after + offset |
| [streetcred.webc:59](src/work/streetcred.webc:59) | before + after + offset |
| [thegroundwork.webc:26](src/work/thegroundwork.webc:26) | before + after + offset |
| [osx-apps-with-js.webc:63](src/work/osx-apps-with-js.webc:63) | before + offset (no after) |

Each has a matching stylesheet: `colorme.css`, `limbo.css`, `streetcred.css`, `groundwork.css`, `osx-apps-with-js.css`.

**How each one customizes the slabs:**

- **colorme** — dust-texture background, `clip-path` polygon for a skewed edge, `::after` rotated 1° and right-anchored
- **groundwork** — accent + dust, long `clip-path` polygon making a torn/jagged bottom edge
- **limbo** — accent + dust on both, `::after` skewed 1.75°
- **streetcred** — pattern background `cover`, `::after` uses an SVG `mask` for a squiggle cut in the page background color
- **jxa** — accent + dust, `::before` at full height, no `::after`

## Not on the system

**What changed:**

- `ul` went from `display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap` to `display: grid` with `grid-auto-rows: 1fr`. That's what equalizes every block — `1fr` rows in an auto-height grid all resolve to the tallest row's height. No fixed value.

It's `contrast-color()`. Returns black or white — whichever contrasts better with what you pass it.

```css
color: contrast-color(#8e42f5);        /* → white */
color: contrast-color(var(--limbo));   /* → black */
```

Works with `attr()`, which lines up with your work-nav:

```css
a {
  background-color: attr(data-bg type(<color>), var(--color-accent-primary));
  color: contrast-color(attr(data-bg type(<color>)));
}
```

Verified against your palette:

| | picks |
|---|---|
| `#8e42f5` streetcred | white |
| `#b42e8a` colorme | white |
| `#3b6fd8` groundwork | white |
| `#151414` jxa | white |
| `#dd3535` limbo | **black** |
| `#66fa32` archive | black |
| `#02e77c` pezzos | black |

Two gotchas:

- **Only the one-argument form ships.** `contrast-color(red AA)` and `contrast-color(red max)` both fail `CSS.supports`. So it's black-or-white, no target ratio, no candidate list. The old `color-contrast(red vs white, black)` syntax is dead.
